# The Value of Disagreement: Why Good Meetings Don't End in Consensus

## The Problem with Agreement

There is a quiet failure that happens in conference rooms every day. A team debates a question for an hour, someone offers a compromise, heads nod, and the meeting ends with a warm sense of harmony. Everyone walks out feeling productive. And yet, two weeks later, nothing has changed. The decision that was supposedly made gets relitigated in hallway conversations. The project stalls. People who "agreed" in the meeting quietly pursue the approach they always preferred.

What went wrong? The agreement was never real. It was a performance of agreement—a social ritual that allowed everyone to escape an uncomfortable conversation. The meeting ended with consensus on the surface and confusion underneath.

We tend to treat unanimity as the sign of a successful discussion. If everyone nods, we must have reached the truth. But this intuition is backwards. Agreement can be a symptom of a deeper problem: nobody has been forced to articulate what they actually believe, or why, or what would change their mind. A meeting that ends in easy harmony may simply be a meeting that never got specific enough to reveal the disagreement hiding inside it.
